intro: This last unit brings the course together. First you will compare three very different societies, Germany, Japan and Mexico, on family, class, government, religion and what their own people say they value. You will see how each one faces shared challenges: paying for care through a welfare state, growing older as fewer children are born, and moving into giant cities.

Comparing whole societies is powerful and risky. Done well, it shows what is common to people everywhere and what is shaped by history and choice. Done badly, it turns real patterns into stereotypes. You will practice using evidence, words like many and on average, and the voices of people describing their own lives.

Then you will do the work historians and political scientists do. You will choose an open question, gather evidence from at least two regions, state the strongest case from both the left and the right, build a claim with evidence and reasoning, and answer the best objection. By the end you will be able to present an argument that is honest about the evidence and fair to people who disagree.
bigQuestion: What can careful comparison of societies teach us, and how do we turn that evidence into a fair, honest argument?

title: World Cultures Today, and Capstone

chapters.title: Europe, Asia and the Americas Compared
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we compare whole societies fairly without flattening the people who live in them?

story.title: Eighteen in Three Places
story.kicker: Three exchange students at a Chicago-area high school discover that turning eighteen means different things at home.
paragraphs: It is lunch in the cafeteria of a high school outside Chicago. Three exchange students share a table this year. Lena is from Leipzig, in eastern Germany. Haruto is from Osaka, in Japan. Sofía is from Guadalajara, in western Mexico. A teacher has asked them one question for a class project: what does your family expect of you at eighteen?

Lena answers first. At eighteen she can vote, sign contracts and move out, and many of her friends will. Her older brother chose a three-year apprenticeship as an electrician instead of university. He is paid while he trains, and her parents call that a smart path. What they expect most, Lena says, is that she stands on her own feet.

Haruto laughs. In Japan the legal age of adulthood dropped from twenty to eighteen in 2022, but his parents still talk about the coming-of-age ceremony. What they expect most is effort on the university entrance exams. His grandmother lives with his family, and he is expected to help care for her. He says the word for it is responsibility, not obedience.

Sofía says her family threw her a big quinceañera at fifteen, with cousins from three states. At eighteen she can vote in Mexico too. But no one expects her to move out soon. Many young adults she knows live at home until they marry or find steady work. What her family expects most, she says, is that she stays close and helps the family move forward together.

Then all three notice something. Each has a friend at home whose family is nothing like theirs. Lena has a friend who lives with her grandmother. Haruto has a cousin who skipped university to start a business. Sofía has a friend who moved alone to Mexico City at seventeen. Their teacher smiles. That, she says, is the first rule of comparing societies.
story.think: What patterns did the three students notice, and why do their friends at home matter when we compare whole countries?

lessons.title: Family Across Three Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Germany, Japan and Mexico all value family, but they differ in household size, living arrangements and what adult children owe their parents.
reading: Picture three dinner tables. In a German apartment, two parents and one teenager eat together. In a Japanese home, a grandmother sits with her son, his wife and their child. In a Mexican house, aunts, cousins and grandparents drop by on Sunday. None of these scenes is the whole story of a country. But each reflects a real pattern that census data show.

A *household* is the group of people who live under one roof. German households are small on average, and many adults live alone, especially in big cities. Japan has long had a tradition of the *extended family*, where three generations share a home. That pattern has shrunk as young people move to cities, yet many older Japanese still live with or near a grown child. Mexican households are larger on average, and relatives often live close by and share child care.

Duties inside families differ too. In Japan, caring for aging parents has been treated as a key duty, often falling on a daughter or daughter-in-law. In Mexico, *familismo* describes a strong sense of loyalty and mutual help among relatives. In Germany, the state pays for more of the care of the old and the young, so families lean less on each other for money. Supporters of each pattern point to its strengths, and critics point to the strain on some members, often women.

words.d: the group of people who live together under one roof
a family that includes grandparents, aunts, uncles or cousins, not just parents and children
a Spanish term for strong loyalty, closeness and mutual help among relatives

look.title: Three Sunday Afternoons
look.text: Scene A: a woman in Hamburg video-calls her mother, then goes hiking with friends. Scene B: a man in Nagoya drives his father to a doctor, then eats lunch with him. Scene C: a teenager in Puebla helps her aunt cook for twelve relatives. Each scene is common in its country, and each also happens in the other two countries.
look.prompt: Which scene fits the pattern described for each country, and what would you need to know before saying a scene is typical?

check.q: What does the term household mean?
choices: All the relatives a person has anywhere
The group of people who live together under one roof
A family that owns its own home
check.why: A household is defined by living together, not by how many relatives someone has.

check.q: Which country in the reading has larger average households with relatives often sharing child care?
check.why: The reading says Mexican households are larger on average and relatives often share child care.

check.q: Why do German families lean less on each other for money, according to the reading?
choices: The state pays for more care of the old and the young
German law forbids living with parents
German families have no older members
Most Germans live in the countryside
check.why: The reading links the difference to the state paying for more care, not to a lack of family feeling.

lessons.title: Class and Getting Ahead
lessons.mainIdea: Each society offers different main roads to a good job: apprenticeships in Germany, exam-based schooling in Japan, and a mix of formal and informal work in Mexico.
reading: Lena's brother trains as an electrician. Three days a week he works at a company, and two days he studies at a vocational school. This is Germany's *dual system* of training. A large share of young Germans choose it, and skilled trades carry real respect. Supporters say it gives many young people a steady path without a university degree. Critics say students are sorted into tracks too early, at around age ten in many states, which can lock in class differences.

In Japan, the main road runs through schools and exams. Getting into a well-known university has long led to jobs at large companies. Many of those jobs once promised *lifetime employment*, meaning a worker could stay with one firm until retirement. That promise has weakened since the 1990s. Today almost four in ten Japanese workers hold part-time or temporary jobs, with lower pay and less security.

In Mexico, a large share of people work in the *informal economy*: street vendors, small family shops and day laborers who pay no payroll taxes and get no official benefits. Mexico's statistics agency, INEGI, counts a little over half of workers this way. Some informal businesses thrive, and some owners prefer the freedom. But informal workers often lack health coverage and pensions, which makes moving up harder. Economists debate whether lower taxes, easier rules or stronger enforcement would help most.

words.d: Germany's training model that combines paid work at a company with classes at a vocational school
a practice at some large Japanese firms of keeping workers from school until retirement
work that is not registered with the government, so it pays no payroll taxes and gets no official benefits
the movement of people up or down between classes during their lives or across generations

look.title: Three Paths at Nineteen
look.text: Jonas in Stuttgart is in the second year of a paid apprenticeship as a car mechanic. Aiko in Sendai is studying for a second try at a university entrance exam. Diego in Monterrey sells phone cases from a stall his uncle runs, and takes night classes in accounting.
look.prompt: For each young person, name the road to a job described in the reading, and one thing that could help or block their social mobility.

check.q: What is Germany's dual system?
choices: Training that combines paid company work with vocational school classes
A school day split between two languages
A rule that everyone attends university twice
check.why: The dual system pairs work at a company with classes at a vocational school.

check.q: What does the reading say has happened to lifetime employment in Japan?
choices: It became required by law in 2022
It has weakened since the 1990s, and many workers now hold part-time or temporary jobs
It spread to all small businesses
check.why: The reading says the promise weakened after the 1990s and almost four in ten workers now hold non-regular jobs.

check.q: Which worker is part of the informal economy?
choices: A street vendor who pays no payroll taxes and gets no official benefits
A teacher at a public school
An apprentice registered with a German company
A bank clerk with a pension plan
check.why: Informal work is not registered with the government, so it carries no payroll taxes or official benefits.

lessons.title: How Each Country Governs
lessons.mainIdea: Germany, Japan and Mexico are all democracies, but they organize power differently: a federal parliamentary system, a parliamentary monarchy and a federal presidential republic.
reading: After defeat in World War II, both Germany and Japan wrote new constitutions. West Germany adopted its *Basic Law* in 1949, and it became the constitution of all Germany at reunification in 1990. Germany is a federal republic of sixteen states. Voters elect the Bundestag, the national parliament, and it chooses the chancellor, who leads the government. The Basic Law opens by protecting human dignity, a direct answer to the crimes of the Nazi years.

Japan's constitution took effect in 1947. It keeps the emperor, but only as a symbol of the state with no power to govern. This is a *constitutional monarchy*. Voters elect the Diet, the two-house parliament, and the Diet chooses the prime minister. One party, the Liberal Democratic Party, has led Japan for most years since 1955. Supporters see stability; critics see too little competition.

Mexico's constitution dates from 1917, after the Mexican Revolution. Mexico is a federal republic with a *presidential system*: voters elect the president directly, separate from Congress. A president serves one six-year term and can never run again, a rule born from anger at long-ruling leaders. For most of the twentieth century one party, the PRI, won every presidential election. In 2000 a candidate from another party won, and Mexico's elections became openly competitive.

words.d: Germany's constitution, adopted in 1949 and extended to the whole country in 1990
a system with a king, queen or emperor whose powers are limited or only symbolic, while elected leaders govern
a government in which voters elect the president separately from the legislature
a system that divides power between a national government and state or regional governments

look.title: The First Line of Germany's Constitution
look.text: Human dignity cannot be violated. Every part of the state's power has a duty to respect it and protect it.
look.cite: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, Article 1, 1949 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might a country that had just lived through the Nazi years choose to begin its constitution with this idea?

check.q: In which country do voters elect the president directly for a single six-year term?
check.why: Mexico's presidential system limits the president to one six-year term.

check.q: What role does Japan's emperor have under the 1947 constitution?
choices: He writes the laws with the Diet
He is a symbol of the state with no power to govern
check.why: Japan is a constitutional monarchy in which the emperor is only a symbol.

check.q: Who chooses Germany's chancellor?
choices: The president of the European Union
check.why: In Germany's parliamentary system the Bundestag elects the chancellor.

lessons.title: Culture in Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Festivals, food and shared customs show what a culture honors, and each one changes over time as people remake it.
reading: In early November, families across Mexico build *ofrendas*, home altars with marigolds, photographs, candles and a loved one's favorite foods. This is the Day of the Dead. It honors ancestors with joy as well as grief. UNESCO added it to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage in 2008. In Chicago, the National Museum of Mexican Art in the Pilsen neighborhood hosts a large Day of the Dead exhibition each year.

In Japan, many families travel home in summer for Obon, when ancestors' spirits are welcomed back with lanterns and dances. In Germany, towns fill with Christmas markets in December, with wooden stalls, mulled drinks and carols. Each of these is a *tradition*, a custom handed down across generations. Notice that all three honor family and memory, even though they look very different.

Traditions are not frozen. Many Japanese couples now hold Western-style wedding ceremonies. German Christmas markets draw tourists who are not Christian. The Day of the Dead grew more widely known after films and parades spread its images. Scholars call this *cultural change*. Some people welcome it as living culture; others worry that meaning is lost when customs become commercial.

words.d: home altars built for the Day of the Dead, with photos, flowers, candles and food for loved ones who have died
a custom or belief handed down from one generation to the next
the way customs, beliefs and ways of life shift over time as people borrow, adapt or drop them

look.title: Three Festivals, One Thread
look.text: Mexico: marigold petals lead from the door to an altar with a grandfather's photo. Japan: a family lights a small fire at the gate to guide ancestors home for Obon. Germany: a family visits a Christmas market together, the way grandparents did decades ago.
look.prompt: What value do these three scenes share, and how does each tradition express it in its own way?

check.q: What is an ofrenda?
choices: A home altar for the Day of the Dead
check.why: Ofrendas are altars with photos, flowers and food honoring loved ones who have died.

check.q: Which festival welcomes ancestors' spirits back home in summer?
check.why: Obon is the Japanese summer festival that welcomes ancestors home.

check.q: According to the reading, what do some people worry about when traditions change?
choices: That no one will travel home
That meaning is lost when customs become commercial
That UNESCO will remove them from its list
check.why: The reading says some worry that commercial versions lose the meaning of the custom.

lessons.title: Welfare States Compared
lessons.mainIdea: A welfare state uses taxes to protect people against illness, old age and job loss, and countries differ sharply in how much they do and who pays.
reading: In the 1880s, German chancellor Otto von Bismarck created the world's first national social insurance: health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old-age pensions in 1889. Bismarck was a conservative. He hoped the programs would win workers away from socialist parties. His model still shapes Germany, where workers and employers pay into insurance funds. This is one type of *welfare state*, a government that protects people against life's major risks.

The Danish scholar Gøsta Esping-Andersen, in a famous 1990 book, sorted rich democracies into three types. Liberal welfare states, like the United States, offer more modest help and rely more on markets. Conservative welfare states, like Germany, tie benefits to work and family. Social democratic welfare states, like Sweden, offer broad benefits to everyone, paid for with high taxes. Japan borrowed from several models and also leans on large companies and families.

Mexico created its social security institute, the IMSS, in 1943 for workers in formal jobs. Because so many work informally, millions were left out. In 1997 Mexico launched Progresa, which paid poor families cash if their children attended school and had health checkups. It became a model copied in many countries. Supporters of big welfare states say they reduce poverty and fear. Critics say high *social spending* can slow growth, raise debt and weaken the habit of self-reliance. Economists still debate how large the trade-offs are.

words.d: a government that uses taxes to protect people against risks such as illness, old age, disability and job loss
programs that workers and employers pay into, which then pay benefits when someone is sick, old or out of work
the money a government spends on pensions, health care, family support and other social programs
a program that gives poor families money if they meet conditions such as keeping children in school

look.title: Public Social Spending
look.cite: OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX), early 2020s, rounded
look.prompt: About how many times more of its economy does Germany spend on social programs than Mexico, and what reasons from the reading might explain the gap?

check.q: Why did Bismarck, a conservative, create social insurance in the 1880s?
choices: To prepare Germany for a war with Japan
To obey a law passed by the European Union
To copy a program from Mexico
To win workers away from socialist parties
check.why: The reading says Bismarck hoped the programs would draw workers away from the socialists.

check.q: In Esping-Andersen's three types, which kind offers broad benefits to everyone, paid for with high taxes?
check.why: Social democratic welfare states, like Sweden, give broad benefits funded by high taxes.

check.q: What was Mexico's Progresa program?
choices: Cash for poor families if children attended school and had health checkups
A pension only for government workers
A training program for German apprentices
check.why: Progresa was a conditional cash transfer that tied payments to school and health visits.

lessons.title: Aging Societies
lessons.mainIdea: Japan and much of Europe are aging fast because people live longer and have fewer children, which strains pensions and care.
reading: In some rural Japanese towns, schools have closed for lack of children while clinics are full of older patients. Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world. About three in ten Japanese people are 65 or older. The average woman in Japan has about 1.2 children in her lifetime. A population needs about 2.1 to replace itself over time. This number is called the *replacement rate*.

The *fertility rate* is the average number of children a woman has. It has dropped below the replacement rate across Europe and East Asia. South Korea's rate fell below 1.0, the lowest in the world. Germany's is about 1.4. Mexico's has fallen too, to below 2.0, but Mexico is still a much younger country, with a median age around thirty. Japan's median age is near fifty.

An aging society has fewer workers paying taxes for each retiree drawing a pension. This is measured by the *dependency ratio*. Countries respond in different ways. Germany has raised its retirement age and relies more on immigration. Japan has invested in robots for care work and accepted more foreign workers, though more cautiously. Some leaders favor paying families to have children; others favor immigration; others favor longer working lives. Each choice has supporters and critics.

words.d: the average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime
the fertility rate, about 2.1, at which a population replaces itself without immigration
the number of children and older people compared with the number of working-age people
the age that splits a population in half: half are older and half are younger

look.title: Share of People Aged 65 and Older
look.cite: World Bank, World Development Indicators, from UN population data, about 2023, rounded
look.prompt: Which country has more than three times Mexico's share of older people, and what might that mean for its workers and pensions?

check.q: What is the replacement rate?
choices: The age at which people retire
The fertility rate of about 2.1 at which a population replaces itself
The share of workers who are immigrants
The number of schools that close each year
check.why: The replacement rate is about 2.1 children per woman.

check.q: Which country in the reading is much younger, with a median age around thirty?
check.why: The reading gives Mexico a median age around thirty and Japan near fifty.

check.q: Why does an aging society strain pensions?
choices: There are fewer workers paying taxes for each retiree
Older people pay more taxes than workers
Pensions are illegal in aging countries
Robots cannot pay into insurance funds
check.why: The dependency ratio rises: fewer workers support each person drawing a pension.

lessons.title: The Move to Cities
lessons.mainIdea: Most people in all three countries now live in cities, and giant metro areas like Tokyo and Mexico City bring both opportunity and strain.
reading: Greater Tokyo is the largest metropolitan area on Earth, home to about 37 million people by UN estimates. Trains arrive every few minutes, and millions ride them daily. Greater Mexico City holds over 20 million people. It sits on an old lakebed, and heavy pumping of groundwater has made parts of the city sink. *Urbanization* is the growth in the share of people who live in cities.

People move to cities for jobs, schools and hospitals. In Mexico, large numbers moved from farms to cities during the twentieth century. Many built homes themselves on the edges of cities, in *informal settlements* that later gained roads, water and titles. Germany urbanized earlier, during the 1800s, and its people are spread across many mid-sized cities rather than one giant capital.

Cities bring strain too. Housing costs rise, commutes lengthen and air can grow dirty. At the same time, the countryside can empty out. Japan now has thousands of empty rural houses, called akiya. Planners argue over the fixes. Some want more public housing and transit; others want fewer building rules so the market can add homes faster. A *megacity* of over ten million people needs both good planning and room to grow.

words.d: the growth in the share of a population that lives in cities
neighborhoods built by residents without official permits, often on the edge of a growing city
a metropolitan area with more than ten million people

look.title: Share of People Living in Cities
look.cite: United Nations, World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision, rounded
look.prompt: All three countries are more urban than the world as a whole. Using the reading, give one reason Germany's share is lower than Japan's even though it urbanized earlier.

check.q: What is urbanization?
choices: The growth in the share of people who live in cities
The rule that cities cannot grow
check.why: Urbanization means a rising share of people living in cities.

check.q: Which is the largest metropolitan area on Earth, by UN estimates?
check.why: The reading names Greater Tokyo, at about 37 million people.

check.q: What are informal settlements?
choices: Neighborhoods built by residents without official permits
check.why: Informal settlements are built without permits, often on a city's edge, and may later gain services.

lessons.title: Religion and Tradition Today
lessons.mainIdea: Religion shapes all three societies, but in different ways: church membership in Germany, practice without membership in Japan, and strong Catholic faith in Mexico.
reading: Every December 12, millions of pilgrims travel to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City. It is one of the most visited Catholic sites in the world. In Mexico's 2020 census, about 78 percent of people called themselves Catholic, and a growing share named Protestant churches or no religion. Faith shapes holidays, family events and many people's sense of what Mexico is.

In Germany, members of registered churches pay a *church tax*, collected by the state along with income tax. Leaving a church ends the tax, and many Germans have left. By the early 2020s, fewer than half of Germans belonged to the Catholic or Protestant church. Germany is also home to millions of Muslims, many from families that came from Turkey as workers from the 1960s on.

Japan looks different again. Most Japanese tell surveys they do not belong to a religion. Yet many visit a Shinto shrine at New Year and hold Buddhist funerals. Scholars say Japanese religion is often about *practice*, what people do, more than *belief*, what people say they believe. This is a reminder that a label like secular can mean different things in different places.

words.d: a tax that members of registered churches pay in Germany, collected by the state
what people do in religion, such as rituals, festivals and visits to holy places
what people hold to be true about God, gods or the meaning of life
not connected to religion, or not tied to religious authority

look.title: Two Ways to Measure Religion
look.text: Survey A asks: Do you belong to a religion? Survey B asks: In the past year, did you visit a shrine, temple or church, or take part in a religious ceremony? In Japan, many people answer no to Survey A and yes to Survey B.
look.prompt: Which survey question tells you more about religion in Japan, and why could the answer differ in Mexico or Germany?

check.q: About what share of Mexicans called themselves Catholic in the 2020 census?
check.why: The reading gives about 78 percent, from Mexico's 2020 census.

check.q: What happens when a German leaves a registered church?
choices: They stop paying the church tax
They lose the right to vote
They must pay a higher income tax
check.why: The church tax is paid by members, so leaving the church ends it.

check.q: What do scholars mean when they say Japanese religion is often about practice more than belief?
choices: Japanese people practice only one religion
Many people take part in rituals even if they do not claim a religion
check.why: Many Japanese visit shrines and hold Buddhist funerals while saying they have no religion.

lessons.title: What Each Society Values
lessons.mainIdea: The fairest way to learn what a society values is to listen to how its own people describe it, through surveys, writing and conversation.
reading: Since 1981, the World Values Survey has asked people in about one hundred countries the same questions. How important is family? Is it more important for a child to learn obedience or independence? How much do you trust people you do not know? The answers let researchers compare values without relying on outsiders' guesses.

Political scientists Ronald Inglehart and Christian Welzel used the survey to draw a well-known map. One line runs from *traditional values*, stressing religion, family and respect for authority, to secular-rational values. Another runs from survival values, stressing security, to *self-expression values*, stressing free choice. On that map, Japan and Germany rank high on secular-rational values, and Mexico ranks more traditional and high in reported happiness.

Such maps are useful but limited. A country average hides big differences between young and old, city and village, rich and poor. People also describe their values in their own words. Many Japanese speak of harmony and consideration for others. Many Mexicans speak of family and faith. Many Germans speak of order, fairness and reliability. Each of these is a *self-description*, and each is only part of the picture.

words.d: values that stress religion, family ties and respect for authority
values that stress free choice, tolerance and a voice in decisions
how a group of people describes its own values, in its own words

look.title: Reading a Survey Answer
look.text: Imagine a survey finds that 80 percent of people in one country say family is very important, and 60 percent in another country say the same. A student writes: People in the second country do not care about their families.
look.prompt: What is wrong with the student's conclusion, and how would you rewrite it so it matches what the numbers actually show?

check.q: Why do researchers use the World Values Survey to compare countries?
choices: It lists every law in each country
It asks people in many countries the same questions about their own values
It is written by tourists who visited each country
check.why: The survey asks people directly, so comparisons do not rest on outsiders' guesses.

check.q: On the Inglehart-Welzel map, what do self-expression values stress?
choices: Free choice, tolerance and a voice in decisions
check.why: Self-expression values are about free choice and having a voice.

check.q: What is one limit of a country average?
choices: It hides big differences between groups inside the country
It cannot be written as a number
It only counts people over sixty-five
check.why: An average hides differences between young and old, city and village, rich and poor.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Stereotypes
lessons.mainIdea: A fair comparison uses evidence about patterns, names its sources and remembers that individuals differ from the average.
reading: Think back to the three exchange students. Each described a real pattern at home. Each also had a friend whose life broke the pattern. A *stereotype* is a fixed, oversimplified idea that all members of a group are alike. It turns a pattern into a rule and a rule into a judgment about people. Stereotypes can be negative or seemingly positive, and both kinds erase real people.

In a 2009 talk, the Nigerian novelist Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie warned about the danger of a single story. When we hear only one story about a people, she said, that story becomes the only thing we know about them. A careful comparison does the opposite. It asks, Compared with what? How many people? Measured by whom? It uses words like many, most and on average instead of all and always.

*Generalization* is not the enemy. Scholars need patterns to compare societies at all. The skill is to hold a pattern loosely. State what the evidence shows, name the source, and notice the exceptions. Also check your own *cultural lens*, the habits and values you grew up with that shape how you see others. What looks strange from outside often makes good sense to the people inside.

words.d: a fixed, oversimplified idea that all members of a group are the same
a statement about a pattern that holds for many members of a group, supported by evidence
the habits and values from your own upbringing that shape how you see other people

look.title: The Danger of a Single Story
look.text: Show a people as only one thing, over and over, and that is what they become in the listener's mind. A single story creates stereotypes, and the problem is not that they are false but that they are incomplete.
look.cite: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, The Danger of a Single Story, TED talk, 2009 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Adichie says stereotypes are incomplete rather than simply false. Give an example from this chapter where a true pattern could become a single story.

check.q: What is the difference between a generalization and a stereotype?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
A generalization describes a pattern with evidence; a stereotype claims everyone in a group is alike
A generalization is always about one person
check.why: Generalizations describe patterns loosely with evidence; stereotypes turn patterns into fixed rules about everyone.

check.q: What did Adichie warn about in her 2009 talk?
choices: The danger of a single story about a people
The danger of learning too many languages
check.why: Her talk argued that a single story creates incomplete stereotypes.

check.q: Which sentence avoids a stereotype?
choices: Every Japanese family lives with grandparents
On average, Mexican households are larger than German households
check.why: It uses on average and states a measurable pattern instead of a claim about everyone.

review.q: Which country uses a dual system that pairs paid company work with vocational school?
review.why: Germany's dual system is its famous apprenticeship model.

review.q: Who created the world's first national social insurance in the 1880s?
review.why: Bismarck, Germany's conservative chancellor, created health, accident and pension insurance.

review.q: Which country has the highest share of people aged 65 and older in the chapter's data?
review.why: About 29 percent of Japan's people are 65 or older.

review.q: What is a conditional cash transfer, like Mexico's Progresa?
choices: A loan to build informal settlements
Money for poor families who meet conditions such as keeping children in school
review.why: Progresa paid families if children attended school and had health checkups.

review.q: How does Japan's government compare with Mexico's?
choices: Japan's parliament chooses the prime minister; Mexico's voters elect the president directly
Both are ruled by an emperor
review.why: Japan is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Mexico is a presidential federal republic.

review.q: What does the chapter say about religion in Japan?
choices: Most people say they have no religion but take part in shrine and temple rituals
review.why: Japanese religion is often about practice more than stated belief.

review.q: A student writes, All Mexicans live with their grandparents. What is the main problem?
choices: It turns a pattern into a stereotype about everyone
review.why: Words like all turn a pattern into a stereotype; many families differ.

review.q: Why is the World Values Survey a fairer tool than a traveler's impressions?
choices: It is written by government leaders
It asks people in many countries the same questions about their own values
review.why: The survey records how people describe their own values, using the same questions everywhere.

chapters.title: Capstone: A Question, Evidence and Your Argument
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you build an argument that is honest about the evidence and fair to the people who disagree with you?

story.title: The Answer Maya Thought She Knew
story.kicker: A student starts her capstone sure of her answer, and the evidence sends her somewhere new.
paragraphs: Maya chose her capstone question in five minutes: What best helps people move up in life? She already knew the answer. Go to college. Her older cousin had been the first in the family to finish a degree, and now he worked as an engineer. Maya planned to find three studies that agreed with her and be done by Friday.

The first surprise came from Germany. Maya read that many Germans reach steady, well-paid work through apprenticeships, not university. The second came from a set of numbers. Economists had compared how much parents' income predicts their children's income in different countries. Denmark and Canada showed much more movement between generations than the United States. Yet Americans attend college at high rates.

The third surprise was closer to home. A team led by economist Raj Chetty had found that children's chances of moving up varied widely across American cities and counties. Where a child grew up seemed to matter, not only whether they went to college. Maya started a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote: Maybe college is one road, not the only one.

She found strong arguments she had never considered. Some writers on the left pointed to public schools, health care and support for poor families. Some writers on the right pointed to stable families, strong local communities, work and economic growth. Maya noticed that both sides had evidence. Neither side had all of it.

On Friday Maya was not done. She had a better question, a messier answer and twice as many sources. Her teacher read the new page and nodded. You changed your mind because of evidence, she said. That is what this project is for.
story.think: Why is changing your mind because of evidence a strength and not a failure, and what evidence would it take to change yours on a question you care about?

lessons.title: Choosing a Strong Question
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone question is open, arguable and researchable, so reasonable people could answer it differently using evidence.
reading: Compare two questions. When did the Berlin Wall fall? The answer is 1989, and it is settled. Why do some democracies last while others collapse? Historians and political scientists still argue about that one. The first is a fact question. The second is a *research question*: open, worth arguing, and answerable with evidence rather than opinion alone.

This course suggests three kinds of capstone questions. What best helps people move up? Why do some democracies last? What makes an ideology turn extreme? Each has a record to study. The last question, for example, can draw on the Nazi regime and the Holocaust, and on Communist regimes such as the Soviet Gulag system and the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, where about a quarter of the population died between 1975 and 1979.

A good question is also narrow enough to finish. What causes poverty in the world? is too big for a semester. What helped South Korea move from poverty to wealth after the 1950s, compared with Mexico? is a better *scope*. Finally, a good question has more than one serious answer. If only one answer is possible, you do not have an *arguable claim* to make.

words.d: an open question that can be answered with evidence and on which reasonable people might disagree
how wide or narrow a question is; how much ground it tries to cover
a statement that some informed people could reasonably dispute, which you must support with evidence

look.title: Sort the Questions
look.text: 1. In what year did Mexico adopt its current constitution? 2. Is Japan a good country? 3. Why did Weimar Germany's democracy collapse by 1933 while Britain's survived the same Great Depression? 4. How can we solve every problem of inequality on Earth?
look.prompt: Which question makes the best capstone question, and what is wrong with each of the others?

check.q: Which is a research question rather than a fact question?
choices: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
What is the capital of Japan?
Why do some democracies last while others collapse?
How many states does Germany have?
check.why: It is open and arguable; experts still disagree about the answer.

check.q: Why is What causes poverty in the world? a weak capstone question?
choices: Its scope is too big to finish well
It has no evidence at all
It is only about one person
check.why: The reading says the question is too big for a semester, so its scope needs narrowing.

check.q: What makes a claim arguable?
choices: It is a personal feeling no one can check
It is a date everyone agrees on
It is copied from one source
Some informed people could reasonably dispute it
check.why: An arguable claim can be reasonably disputed and must be supported with evidence.

lessons.title: Gathering Evidence From Two Regions
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence from at least two regions lets you test whether a pattern is general or only true in one place.
reading: Suppose your question is what helps people move up. If you study only the United States, you cannot tell whether your answer is about human societies or only about one country. Adding Germany, Japan, Mexico or Denmark lets you compare. This method is called *comparative analysis*: studying cases side by side to see which causes seem to matter.

Sources come in two main kinds. A *primary source* comes from the time or people being studied: a constitution, a census table, a speech or a survey. A *secondary source* is written later by someone interpreting the evidence, like a history book or a research article. Strong projects use both. Primary sources give you the raw record. Secondary sources show how experts have read it.

Check every source. Who made it, and why? Is it published by a known body, such as the OECD, the World Bank, a national statistics office or a university press? Does another source agree? This habit is called *corroboration*. A single striking number shared on social media, with no author or date, is not yet evidence. Find where it came from before you use it.

words.d: studying two or more cases side by side to see which causes or features seem to matter
evidence created by the people or at the time being studied, such as a law, census or speech
a later account that interprets evidence, such as a history book or research article
checking whether other reliable sources agree with a piece of evidence

look.title: How Long to Climb the Ladder?
look.cite: OECD, A Broken Social Elevator? How to Promote Social Mobility, 2018, rounded
look.prompt: The OECD estimated how many generations it would take a child from a low-income family to reach average income. What does comparing five countries show that studying one country could not?

check.q: Which is a primary source?
choices: A blog post summarizing a study
A documentary made fifty years later
check.why: A census table is part of the original record, created at the time being studied.

check.q: Why does the reading recommend evidence from at least two regions?
choices: Because one country never has data
To test whether a pattern is general or only true in one place
check.why: Comparative analysis shows which causes seem to matter across places.

check.q: What is corroboration?
choices: Checking whether other reliable sources agree
Copying a source word for word
Choosing sources that match your view
check.why: Corroboration means confirming evidence with other trustworthy sources.

lessons.title: Reading Numbers Carefully
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers are powerful evidence only when you know what they measure, who measured them and what they cannot show.
reading: Economist Miles Corak compared rich countries using a measure called *intergenerational earnings elasticity*. It shows how strongly a father's earnings predict his son's. A figure near zero means children's earnings barely depend on their parents'. A figure near one means they depend almost entirely on them. In Corak's figures, Denmark scored about 0.15 and the United States about 0.47.

Countries with more income inequality also tended to show less mobility. Economist Alan Krueger named this pattern the Great Gatsby Curve in 2012. It is a *correlation*: two things that rise and fall together. A correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other. Inequality might block mobility, or a third factor, such as school quality or family structure, might drive both.

Read every number with questions. What exactly was measured, and for whom? Corak's data followed fathers and sons, partly because older records tracked men's earnings better. Figures from different studies can use different methods, so compare numbers from the same source when you can. Name the source every time. This is part of *data literacy*, the skill of reading numbers honestly.

words.d: a measure of how strongly parents' earnings predict their children's earnings; higher means less mobility
a pattern in which two things tend to rise or fall together, which does not by itself prove cause
when one thing actually produces a change in another
the skill of reading, questioning and explaining numbers honestly

look.title: How Much Do Fathers' Earnings Predict Sons'?
look.cite: Miles Corak, Income Inequality, Equality of Opportunity, and Intergenerational Mobility, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2013
look.prompt: Which two countries show the least mobility between generations, and what is one reason you should be careful before saying why?

check.q: In Corak's figures, what does a higher elasticity mean?
choices: Children's earnings depend more on their parents'
check.why: Higher elasticity means parents' earnings predict children's more strongly, so there is less mobility.

check.q: What is the Great Gatsby Curve?
choices: A rule that proves inequality causes low mobility
A pattern linking higher inequality with lower mobility across countries
check.why: It is a correlation between inequality and lower mobility, named by Alan Krueger in 2012.

check.q: Why can't a correlation alone prove causation?
choices: A third factor might drive both things
Only one country can be studied at a time
check.why: Something like school quality could cause both patterns, so the link alone does not prove cause.

lessons.title: A Worked Case: Why Democracies Last
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars explain democratic survival with several factors, including wealth, strong institutions and leaders who accept the rules, and they still weigh these differently.
reading: Weimar Germany became a democracy in 1919. By 1933 Adolf Hitler was chancellor, and within months the democracy was gone. India became a democratic republic in 1950 while still very poor, and it has held regular elections since, with a break in civil rights during the Emergency of 1975 to 1977. Chile, one of Latin America's longest-running democracies, fell to a military coup in 1973 and returned to democracy in 1990. These cases make a good puzzle.

One well-known finding comes from political scientist Adam Przeworski and colleagues: democracies in richer countries have rarely collapsed. Wealth seems to help democracy survive once it exists. But India shows that a poor country can sustain democracy, and Weimar shows that a modern, educated country can lose it. So scholars also look at *institutions*, the rules and organizations like courts, parties and a free press.

In their 2018 book How Democracies Die, Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt argued that written rules are not enough. Democracies also depend on *norms*, unwritten habits. Two matter most, they said: *mutual toleration*, treating opponents as legitimate rivals rather than enemies, and forbearance, not using every legal power to the hilt. Other scholars stress economic crisis, war or outside pressure. A strong capstone weighs these explanations rather than picking one without evidence.

words.d: the rules and organizations that shape political life, such as courts, parties, elections and a free press
unwritten habits and expectations that guide how people use power
accepting political opponents as legitimate rivals who have a right to compete and govern
the sudden, illegal seizure of government power, often by the military

look.title: Guardrails of Democracy
look.text: Constitutions alone cannot protect a democracy. It also relies on two unwritten guardrails: rivals accepting each other as legitimate, and leaders holding back from using their full legal power to crush opponents.
look.cite: Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, How Democracies Die, 2018 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: How could the idea of unwritten guardrails help explain why a democracy with a strong written constitution might still fail?

check.q: What does India's history add to the question of why democracies last?
choices: It shows that a poor country can sustain democracy
It proves only rich countries can be democracies
It shows that coups always succeed
It shows India never held elections
check.why: India has kept regular elections since 1950 while starting very poor, which complicates the wealth explanation.

check.q: According to Levitsky and Ziblatt, what are norms?
choices: Unwritten habits and expectations about how power is used
check.why: Norms are the unwritten guardrails, such as mutual toleration and forbearance.

check.q: What happened in Chile in 1973?
choices: Its democracy fell to a military coup
check.why: Chile's long-running democracy was overthrown by a military coup in 1973 and returned in 1990.

lessons.title: The Strongest Case From the Left
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers on the left often argue that opportunity grows when government reduces inequality and invests in schools, health and families.
reading: Take Maya's question: what best helps people move up? Many on the political *left* start from the Nordic countries. Denmark and Norway combine high taxes with free university, strong public schools, paid parental leave and wide health coverage. They also show high mobility in Corak's figures. To left-leaning thinkers, that is no coincidence.

The argument runs like this. Children do not choose their parents. If a poor child lacks good schools, health care or a stable home, talent is wasted. Public spending evens the starting line, the argument goes, and *redistribution*, moving income from richer to poorer people through taxes and benefits, keeps inequality from hardening into a class system. Some point to the Great Gatsby Curve as support.

To represent this side fairly, state it in its strongest form, as its best defenders would. Do not pick its weakest supporter or its worst slogan. Then note its record. The democratic left built much of Europe's welfare states. The far left, in its revolutionary Communist form, also produced the Soviet Gulag and the Great Leap Forward famine in China. Most *social democrats* reject that path and support elections and markets with a strong safety net.

words.d: a broad political direction that tends to favor more equality and a larger role for government in reducing it
moving income or wealth from richer to poorer people through taxes and public programs
people on the democratic left who support elections and markets along with a strong welfare state

look.title: Strong Form or Weak Form?
look.text: Version A: The left just wants to take your money. Version B: Many on the left argue that public schools, health care and family support give poor children a fairer start, and they point to high mobility in Nordic countries as evidence.
look.prompt: Which version represents the left in its strongest form, and why would using the weaker version hurt your own argument?

check.q: What is redistribution?
choices: Moving income from richer to poorer people through taxes and programs
check.why: Redistribution uses taxes and benefits to move income toward poorer people.

check.q: Which countries do many on the left point to as evidence?
choices: The Nordic countries such as Denmark and Norway
check.why: They point to the Nordic mix of high taxes, strong public services and high mobility.

check.q: How do most social democrats differ from revolutionary Communists?
choices: They support elections and markets with a strong safety net
check.why: Social democrats work through elections and accept markets, unlike revolutionary Communist regimes.

lessons.title: The Strongest Case From the Right
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers on the right often argue that opportunity grows from economic growth, strong families and communities, and personal responsibility.
reading: Many on the political *right* start from a different set of cases. South Korea was one of the poorest countries on Earth in the 1950s. Through fast growth driven by exports, hard work and heavy investment in education, it became a rich country within two generations. To right-leaning thinkers, *economic growth* is the most powerful ladder, because it creates jobs and lifts whole societies.

They also point to institutions outside government. Research by Raj Chetty and colleagues found that upward mobility was higher in American areas with more two-parent families, stronger community ties and more civic groups. Conservatives read this as support for strengthening families, churches and local communities. Many on the right also stress personal responsibility and *free markets*, arguing that high taxes and heavy rules can slow growth and discourage work.

Represent this side in its strongest form too, not by its worst slogan. Then note its record. The democratic right built much of the postwar prosperity in West Germany and Japan. The far right, in its Fascist and Nazi forms, produced violent dictatorships, war and the Holocaust. Mainstream *conservatives* reject that path and defend elections, the rule of law and individual rights.

words.d: a broad political direction that tends to favor tradition, free markets and a more limited role for government
an increase in the total amount of goods and services a country produces
an economy in which prices, jobs and businesses are shaped mostly by buyers and sellers rather than government
people on the democratic right who value tradition, stability and gradual change within the law

look.title: Two Readings of One Study
look.text: Chetty's team found that areas with higher upward mobility tended to have less residential segregation, less income inequality, better schools, more two-parent families and stronger community ties. A left-leaning writer highlights inequality and schools. A right-leaning writer highlights families and community.
look.prompt: Both writers cite the same study. What does that tell you about using evidence fairly, and how would you report the study in your own argument?

check.q: Why do many on the right point to South Korea?
choices: It had the world's largest welfare state
It became rich through fast growth driven by exports, work and education
check.why: South Korea's rapid growth from poverty is the right's example of growth as a ladder.

check.q: Which finding from Chetty's research do conservatives stress?
choices: Higher mobility in areas with more two-parent families and stronger community ties
Lower mobility wherever taxes were low
Higher mobility only in the largest cities
check.why: They read the family and community findings as support for strengthening those institutions.

check.q: How do mainstream conservatives differ from Fascists?
choices: They defend elections, the rule of law and individual rights
check.why: Mainstream conservatives work within democracy, unlike Fascist and Nazi regimes.

lessons.title: Knowing the Other Side
lessons.mainIdea: You understand your own position only when you can state the strongest opposing case as well as its supporters can.
reading: In 1859 the English philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote On Liberty. He argued that a person who has only heard one side of a question does not truly understand even their own view. You need to hear opposing arguments from people who actually believe them, at their most persuasive. Only then can you know why your view holds up, if it does.

Today people call this *steelmanning*: building the strongest version of an argument you disagree with. It is the opposite of a *straw man*, a weak, twisted version of the other side that is easy to knock down. A straw man may win applause from people who already agree. It will not convince anyone else, and it leaves your own thinking untested.

A simple test helps. Could a supporter of the other side read your summary of their view and say, Yes, that is what I believe? If so, you have been fair. Watch also for *confirmation bias*, the habit of noticing evidence that fits what you already think and skipping what does not. Maya's early plan to find three studies that agreed with her was confirmation bias at work.

words.d: stating the strongest, fairest version of an argument you disagree with
a weak or twisted version of someone's argument, made so it is easy to attack
the habit of favoring evidence that supports what you already believe

look.title: John Stuart Mill on Hearing Both Sides
look.text: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
look.cite: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter 2, 1859
look.prompt: Explain Mill's sentence in your own words. How would following it change the way you research your capstone question?

check.q: What is a straw man?
choices: The strongest version of an opposing view
A weak or twisted version of someone's argument, easy to attack
check.why: A straw man misrepresents the other side so it is easy to knock down.

check.q: What did Mill argue in On Liberty?
choices: A person who knows only their own side barely understands it
Arguments should be settled by majority vote
check.why: Mill wrote that knowing only your own side means knowing little of it.

check.q: Maya planned to find only studies that agreed with her. What is this called?
check.why: Confirmation bias is favoring evidence that fits what you already believe.

lessons.title: Claim, Evidence and Reasoning
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument states a clear claim, supports it with specific evidence and explains the reasoning that links the two.
reading: Here is a claim Maya might write: Access to paid, recognized job training outside university helps many young people move up. Her evidence: Germany's dual system reaches a large share of young people, and Germany's youth unemployment has stayed lower than many European neighbors'. Her *reasoning*: a paid path with a recognized credential lets students earn while learning, so family money matters less.

In 1958 the British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described the parts of an everyday argument. The *claim* is what you want the reader to accept. The data or *evidence* are the facts that support it. The warrant is the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim. Many classrooms now teach this as claim, evidence and reasoning.

Strong writers also add a *qualifier*, a word that shows how sure they are, such as often, in many cases or probably. Maya's claim says many young people, not all. Qualifiers are not weakness. They are honesty about what the evidence can carry. A claim that is too strong breaks when a reader finds one exception.

words.d: the main point an argument asks the reader to accept
facts, data or sources that support a claim
the explanation of why the evidence supports the claim; Toulmin called it the warrant
a word or phrase, such as often or probably, that shows how strongly a claim is made

look.title: The Parts of an Argument
look.text: An everyday argument moves from data to a claim. What lets us make that step is a warrant, a general rule that links the two. A careful arguer also says how strongly the claim holds, and under what conditions it might not.
look.cite: Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, 1958 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: In Maya's argument about apprenticeships, identify the claim, the data and the warrant.

check.q: In Toulmin's model, what is the warrant?
choices: The main point you want accepted
The reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim
check.why: The warrant is the link between evidence and claim, taught today as reasoning.

check.q: Which word in a claim is a qualifier?
check.why: Often shows how strongly the claim is made, which is what a qualifier does.

check.q: Why does the reading say qualifiers make an argument stronger?
choices: They show honesty about what the evidence can support
They remove the need for sources
check.why: A claim that is too strong breaks at one exception; a qualified claim matches the evidence.

lessons.title: Answering Counterarguments
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument names the best objection to its claim and answers it honestly, by rebutting it, limiting the claim or conceding the point.
reading: A reader of Maya's argument might object: Germany sorts students into school tracks at about age ten, so apprenticeships may lock working-class children out of university. This is a *counterargument*, a reason someone might reject your claim. It is a serious one, raised by German researchers themselves. Ignoring it would make Maya's essay weaker.

There are three honest ways to answer. You can offer a *rebuttal*, evidence that the objection is wrong or smaller than it seems. For example, Germany offers routes from vocational training to later university study. You can narrow your claim so it no longer overreaches. Or you can make a *concession*, admitting the objection has force, and then explain why your claim still holds on balance.

Place the counterargument where a reader would raise it, often after your main evidence. State it fairly, in its strongest form. Answer it with evidence, not with a label or an insult. Readers trust writers who show them the whole field. A capstone that answers the best objection is more persuasive, not less, because the reader can see the claim has been tested.

words.d: a reason or piece of evidence that someone might use to reject your claim
a response showing that a counterargument is wrong or less important than it seems
admitting that part of an opposing argument is true while explaining why your claim still holds

look.title: Three Ways to Answer
look.text: Claim: Conditional cash transfers like Mexico's Progresa help poor children move up. Objection: Paying families might make them depend on government. Response 1: That is a silly worry. Response 2: Studies of Progresa found higher school enrollment, and the payments were tied to school attendance. Response 3: Dependence is a fair concern, so programs should be judged over the long run.
look.prompt: Which response is a rebuttal, which is a concession, and which one should a strong writer never use? Explain.

check.q: What is a counterargument?
choices: A reason someone might reject your claim
check.why: A counterargument is an objection to your claim.

check.q: What is a concession?
choices: Admitting part of an objection is true while explaining why your claim still holds
check.why: A concession grants the objection some force but keeps the claim on balance.

check.q: Why does answering the best objection make an argument more persuasive?
choices: It proves the other side has no evidence
Readers can see the claim has been tested
It avoids the need for a claim
check.why: Readers trust a writer who shows the whole field and tests the claim against it.

lessons.title: Presenting and Discussing Respectfully
lessons.mainIdea: Sharing your argument well means speaking clearly, listening fully and disagreeing with ideas without attacking people.
reading: Maya presents her findings to her class. A classmate, Andre, disagrees: he thinks college is still the surest road up in the United States. Maya does not roll her eyes. She says, Tell me more about your evidence. Andre cites data showing college graduates earn more on average. Maya agrees that the pattern is real, then shares her German and Danish comparisons. Both leave with something new.

This is *civil discourse*: discussion in which people disagree honestly while treating each other with respect. A few habits make it work. Listen to understand, not only to reply. Restate the other person's point before you answer it. Critique the idea, never the person. An *ad hominem* attack, aimed at a person instead of their argument, proves nothing about the argument.

When you present, make it easy to follow. Start with your question and claim. Show two or three pieces of evidence, each with its source named. Give the strongest counterargument and your answer. End with what you still do not know. Visual aids help many listeners. A clear chart or map with a *citation* on it lets your audience check your evidence for themselves.

words.d: honest discussion in which people disagree while treating each other with respect
an attack on a person instead of on their argument
a note naming the author or body, title and year of a source so others can find it

look.title: Two Replies
look.text: A classmate says democracies last mainly because countries are wealthy. Reply A: You only think that because you never read anything. Reply B: So you are saying wealth is the main factor. That fits Przeworski's finding, but how would you explain India, which kept its democracy while still poor?
look.prompt: Which reply practices civil discourse? Name two habits from the reading that it uses.

check.q: What is an ad hominem attack?
choices: An attack on a person instead of their argument
check.why: Ad hominem targets the person, which proves nothing about the argument.

check.q: What did Maya do when Andre disagreed?
choices: She asked about his evidence and acknowledged what was true in it
check.why: She listened, asked for his evidence, agreed the pattern was real and then shared her own.

check.q: Which step belongs at the end of a strong presentation, according to the reading?
choices: Repeating your claim with no evidence
Saying what you still do not know
check.why: The reading says to end with what you still do not know, which is honest about the limits of evidence.

review.q: Which makes the strongest capstone question?
choices: Why did Chile's democracy fall in 1973 while Costa Rica's survived?
How can we fix every problem at once?
review.why: It is open, arguable, researchable and narrow enough to finish.

choices: Stating the strongest, fairest version of a view you disagree with
review.why: Steelmanning represents the other side as its best defenders would.

review.q: What does the Great Gatsby Curve show?
choices: That college always leads to wealth
That countries with more inequality tend to have less mobility
review.why: It is a correlation between inequality and lower mobility across countries.

review.q: Levitsky and Ziblatt argue democracies depend on unwritten norms. Which is one of them?
review.why: Mutual toleration and forbearance are their two key guardrails.

review.q: How do the left and right usually differ on what helps people move up?
choices: The left stresses public investment and less inequality; the right stresses growth, families and markets
The left opposes schools; the right opposes jobs
review.why: Each side emphasizes different causes, and each cites real evidence.

review.q: Which pair names extreme records from both the far left and the far right?
choices: Obon and the Day of the Dead
The Khmer Rouge killings and the Holocaust
The Basic Law and On Liberty
review.why: The Khmer Rouge was a Communist regime and the Holocaust was carried out by the Nazi regime.

review.q: In claim, evidence and reasoning, what does the reasoning do?
choices: Explains why the evidence supports the claim
review.why: Reasoning, Toulmin's warrant, links the evidence to the claim.

review.q: Why should you gather evidence from at least two regions?
choices: To test whether a pattern is general or local
Because one region has no data
To make the claim stronger than the evidence
review.why: Comparative analysis shows whether a cause seems to matter beyond one place.
